metadata.title: The swarm found 266 bugs. Then I checked the axis.
metadata.topic: Anthropic's multiagent coordination experiments — Figures 1, 2 and 3
metadata.purpose: Show that the coordination result is real but that its headline number is not like-for-like, and that its adjudication is unmeasured.
metadata.gate: GATE P — not passed; no audio generated
metadata.reformat: center-cut, focus-aware; pantry/<bid>-916.* is the human replacement slot; -916 overrides honored

beats.narration_text: Hey Claude — Anthropic just put forty-five agents on fifteen open-source codebases and let them talk to each other. Did coordinating actually help?

props.command: Anthropic put 45 agents on 15 open-source codebases and let them coordinate. Did it actually help?
props.segment: The swarm found 266 bugs. Then I checked the axis.
props.runningText: Reading the paper… 45 agents, 27M tokens, 266 findings.

beats.new_visual_element: composer prompt, Liam's ask

beats.narration_text: Short answer: yes. Long answer: not by the number they printed. Let's read the chart.

artifactLines: The coordination result is real.
The headline number is not like-for-like.
Let's read the chart.

beats.new_visual_element: verdict stub — 'yes, but not by 12.7x'

beats.narration_text: This is the chart they published.
beats.credit: Anthropic Frontier Red Team, 'Patterns and problems in emerging multiagent systems', 13 Aug 2026 — published figure, reproduced for criticism
beats.new_visual_element: the published Figure 1, as Anthropic drew it

beats.narration_text: Two hundred sixty-six vulnerabilities from the swarm. Twenty-one from the parallel run. Twelve point seven times more findings. That is the number that will get quoted.
beats.credit: Anthropic Frontier Red Team, 'Patterns and problems in emerging multiagent systems', 13 Aug 2026 — published figure, reproduced for criticism
beats.new_visual_element: hold on the 266 vs 21 labels

beats.narration_text: Now watch what happens when you make the two runs comparable.

production_viz.label: animated Figure 1 — the like-for-like correction
production_viz.note: silent 3840x2160 master, born native 4K; audit annotation already burned in

beats.new_visual_element: animated Figure 1 — the like-for-like correction

beats.narration_text: Credit where it is due: the correction is in the post. The headline just isn't.

artifactLines: Limit the swarm's outputs to core directories,
and the two methods seem comparable
in tokens per vulnerability found.

beats.credit: Anthropic Frontier Red Team, 13 Aug 2026 — verbatim text from the archived page, reproduced for criticism. Stylesheet was not archived; excerpt is typeset in the house serif, wording unaltered.
beats.new_visual_element: the concession, in Anthropic's own words

beats.narration_text: There is a bigger problem and it is not about tokens. What is a vulnerability here? Whatever the arbiter agent said was new and valid.

artifactLines: What counts as a vulnerability?
Whatever the arbiter agent said was new and valid.
Same model family. No human triage.

beats.new_visual_element: the arbiter loop — LLM judging LLMs

beats.narration_text: That is the load-bearing assumption of the whole experiment. Everything downstream of it inherits the uncertainty.

artifactLines: The fifteen projects are never named.
The arbiter's error rate is unmeasured.
All downstream results depend on this.

beats.new_visual_element: weakest-link card

beats.narration_text: Second experiment. Same idea, harder problem: build a text-based open-world game, twelve hours, agents must actually depend on each other.

props.artifactHeading: Build a text game in 12 hours
artifactLines: Agents must genuinely depend on each other.
Shared codebase. Dependency graph required.
Real coordination under time pressure.

beats.new_visual_element: the game-build brief

beats.narration_text: The games were bad. Anthropic says so plainly — inscrutable interfaces, brutal learning curves, too slow to play. That is not the interesting part.

props.artifactHeading: "Models have poor taste in this arena"
artifactLines: Inscrutable interfaces.
Brutal learning curves.
Too slow to play.

beats.new_visual_element: quote — 'models have poor taste in this arena'

beats.narration_text: The interesting part is this pair of charts. Left: what fraction of pull requests got merged. Right: how much of an agent's files were written by somebody else.
beats.credit: Anthropic Frontier Red Team, 'Patterns and problems in emerging multiagent systems', 13 Aug 2026 — published figure, reproduced for criticism
beats.new_visual_element: published Figure 2 — merge fraction and code sharing

beats.narration_text: The story Anthropic tells is that only Sonnet 5 keeps a high merge rate while genuinely sharing code. Look at the right-hand axis.
beats.credit: Anthropic Frontier Red Team, 'Patterns and problems in emerging multiagent systems', 13 Aug 2026 — published figure, reproduced for criticism
beats.new_visual_element: hold on the right panel's 0.25 axis ceiling

beats.narration_text: It tops out at zero point two five. Put both panels on the same zero-to-one scale and the collaboration story changes shape.

production_viz.label: animated Figure 2 — both panels on the same 0-1 axis
production_viz.note: silent 3840x2160 master, born native 4K; audit annotation already burned in

beats.new_visual_element: animated Figure 2 — both panels on the same 0-1 axis

beats.narration_text: So the claim is true — at twenty, forty, and eighty agents. It is false at ten. And the thing it describes is small.

props.artifactHeading: True at scale. False at ten.
artifactLines: Sonnet 5 leads at 20, 40, and 80 agents.
At 10 agents: the oldest model shares more.
The effect is real and small.

beats.new_visual_element: true-at-scale / false-at-10 card

beats.narration_text: Third chart. Pull requests opened and merged over a twelve-hour run.
beats.credit: Anthropic Frontier Red Team, 'Patterns and problems in emerging multiagent systems', 13 Aug 2026 — published figure, reproduced for criticism
beats.new_visual_element: published Figure 3 — PR activity over 12 hours

beats.narration_text: Older models look terrible here. Opus 4.6 opened nine hundred eighty pull requests and merged about ninety. That is a nine percent hit rate, and it looks like chaos.

production_viz.label: animated Figure 3 — opened vs merged, per model
production_viz.note: silent 3840x2160 master, born native 4K; audit annotation already burned in

beats.new_visual_element: animated Figure 3 — opened vs merged, per model

beats.narration_text: Mythos Preview merged seventy-eight percent. Enormous improvement. It also opened one hundred sixty-nine pull requests instead of nine hundred eighty.

production_viz.label: 169 vs 980 — the volume collapse
production_viz.note: silent 3840x2160 master, born native 4K; audit annotation already burned in

beats.new_visual_element: 169 vs 980 — the volume collapse

beats.narration_text: The newest model does eighty-three percent less work and merges a higher fraction of it. On this chart, solving coordination and quietly doing less are the same line.

props.artifactHeading: Solved coordination — or just did less?
artifactLines: Reading 1: Mythos Preview solved conflict.
Reading 2: It opened 169 PRs instead of 980.
On this chart, they are the same line.

beats.new_visual_element: the two readings of one line, side by side

beats.narration_text: One more thing from this half of the post, and it has no figure at all — which is a shame, because it may be the most consequential claim in the piece.

props.artifactHeading: The most consequential claim has no chart
artifactLines: Agents are low variance.
Same model, same context, same choice.
The post describes it. Doesn't measure it.

beats.new_visual_element: the no-figure flag

beats.narration_text: And in a pricing game, given a private channel, they colluded by round three. Take the channel away and they still colluded — price-matching to the penny off a public board.

artifactLines: wholesale is 10 for all of us,
so a price war just burns everyone’s margin...
happy to coordinate who covers which niches.
